newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Iran-S.Africa oil depot deal not ready for signing.
newsitem.headline: Iran-S.Africa oil depot deal not ready for signing.

text.p: Iran's President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani will discuss plans to store Iranian crude oil in South Africa during a state visit this week, but nothing will be signed yet, officials said on Wednesday.
"No deals or agreements will be signed during the visit," said South African foreign ministry spokesman Enrico Kemp. Rafsanjani, on a tour of African states, arrives on Thursday.

The proposal to store at least 15 million barrels of Iranian oil at the Central Energy Fund's (CEF) 45-million barrel depot at Saldanha Bay, north of Cape Town, has been delayed for an environmental impact study.

That study is not expected to be completed much before the end of the year. But the CEF said in its 1995/6 annual report this week that it expected to be storing and trading the crude by March next year.
Other proposals which may be considered are a joint venture to develop Iran's natural gas fields, and Iranian cooperation in developing South Africa's oil refining sector.
Iran has the second-largest natural gas reserves in the world after Russia and is keen to develop them in order to diversify its economy and limit its heavy dependence on oil.
Kemp added that the broad focus of Rafsanjani's whistle-stop state visit on Thursday and Friday would be to strengthen bilateral relations and rectify a trade imbalance.

South Africa historically depends on Iran for two-thirds of its crude oil, for which it pays about five billion rand ($1.12 billion) annually, while Iran last year bought South African goods worth only 145.7 million rand ($32.5 million).

However, Iran's dominance of the South African oil market has been challenged this year by a strong marketing drive by Kuwait while oil buyers have increasingly been turning to other sources since the lifting of the anti-apartheid oil embargo.

"Iran still dominates for historical reasons, but South African refineries are configured for Middle Eastern crudes and Kuwait does have an edge...Buyers are entirely driven by economics," one oil industry analyst said.
Kemp said Iran was also looking at diversifying imports from South Africa to include paper pulp, mining technology and expertise, and agricultural products such as sugar.

But Rafsanjani's six-nation swing through Africa, which also aims to win support for the Iranian government in the face of repeated U.S. accusations that Tehran is sponsoring terrorism, is expected to be frowned on by Washington.
The tour comes a month after U.S. President Bill Clinton tightened sanctions against Iran with a law penalising non-U.S. firms investing $40 million or more in Iran or Libya.
Washington has made it clear on several occasions that it disapproves of the warming relations between Pretoria and Tehran since the election of President Nelson Mandela in 1994.

But international relations analyst Larry Benjamin of the University of Witwatersrand told South African radio that while the U.S. would continue to voice criticism, "ultimately I don't think there's any real action that the United States can take".
